title: The do while Loop
description: A loop that runs its block first and asks the question afterwards, so it always runs at least once.

content.value: A `while` loop tests first, so it can run zero times. A `do while` loop runs the body first and tests after, so it always runs **at least once**.

content.real: Tasting soup, then deciding if it needs more salt
content.text: You cannot decide whether to taste again until you have tasted once. In the same way, you cannot decide to ask the user again until you have asked once.

content.title: Same false condition, different result
content.caption: `while` looked before it leapt, and did not leap. `do while` leapt once, then looked.

parts.label: condition
parts.note: Tested after each turn. True: go round again.

parts.label: semicolon
parts.note: Required. The `while (...)` here ends a statement, it does not start a block.

content.title: How a do while ends
content.caption: It is the only C++ loop that ends with a semicolon.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: The body prints `n`, then doubles it: 1, 2, 4, 8. After 8 it becomes 16, and `16 < 10` is false, so 16 is never printed.

content.value: Asking Until the Answer Is Sensible
Input checking is where `do while` shines. With `while`, you wrote the question twice. With `do while`, you write it once.

do while
items.text: Written once, and asked at least once.

content.title: Validating a score
content.caption: The do while version has one prompt and one read, so the two copies can never drift apart when you edit one of them.

content.value: Declare `int score;` above the loop so the condition and the lines after it can see it. Leaving it without a value is safe only because the body always runs and `cin` fills it first. C++ will not stop you reading a variable with no value: you get a leftover garbage number.
content.title: A variable with no value

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: `tries` becomes 1, 2, then 3. Then `3 < 3` is false and the loop stops. A do while counter can never end at 0, because one turn is unavoidable.

content.value: The other classic use is a menu. Show the options, do what was chosen, then show them again, until the user picks quit.

content.title: One turn of the menu loop
content.caption: The `else if` chain from Module 4 does the deciding. The loop does the coming back.
Sample run: type 1 (prints `Hello!`), then 0 (prints `Goodbye.`). The `else if (choice != 0)` catch-all stops quitting from printing "I do not know option 0".

content.value: A `switch` from Module 4 works just as well inside the loop. Its `break` only leaves the `switch`, not the loop, which is exactly what you want here.
content.title: switch works too

items.sub: You know the number of turns before you start.
The number of turns might be zero.
It must run at least once: menus and input checks.

content.title: Ask: how many times should the body run?

steps.note: `i` starts at 1. `1 <= 0` is false, so the body is skipped. Zero turns.
`0 > 0` is false. The `while` body is skipped too.
`do` goes straight into the body without testing.
Now test `0 > 0`: false. The loop ends after one turn.

content.title: Three loops, nothing to do
content.outro: Only the `do while` printed. On data that might be empty, a `do while` will process the thing that is not there.

content.value: `do while` is the least used of the three. Reach for it for menus and input checks, and use `for` or `while` for everything else.

quiz.question: What is the one real difference between `while` and `do while`?
options: A do while can only count upwards
A do while tests its condition after the block, so the block always runs at least once
A do while does not need a condition
quiz.explain: Everything else about them is the same. The order of block and test is the whole difference.

quiz.question: How many times does `do { cout << "hi" << endl; } while (false);` print?
quiz.explain: The block runs before the condition is ever looked at, so a condition that is false from the start still allows one turn.

quiz.question: What is easy to forget when writing a do while loop?
quiz.explain: It is the only loop that ends with a semicolon, because that final `while (...)` completes a statement instead of opening a block.

quiz.question: Why is a do while loop a good fit for input validation?
options: It stops the user typing letters
You have to ask once before you can know whether to ask again
It is faster than a while loop
quiz.explain: The first question is unavoidable, so a loop that always runs once lets you write the prompt and the rule a single time.

quiz.question: Why must the variable tested by a do while loop be declared above the `do`?
options: do while cannot use int variables
Because it has to be const
The condition sits outside the block, so a variable declared inside is already gone
quiz.explain: Anything declared inside the braces stops existing at the closing brace, and the condition comes after that closing brace.
